'''John M. J. Madey''' (28 February 1943<ref>{{cite web|title=John Michael Julius Madey|url=https://physicstoday.scitation.org/doi/10.1063/PT.3.3436|publisher=PHYSICS TODAY|date=1 January 2017|access-date=19 July 2019}}</ref> - 5 July 2016<ref>{{cite web|title=In Memoriam: Physicist and inventor John Madey|url=http://www.hawaii.edu/news/2016/07/20/in-memoriam-physicist-and-inventor-john-madey/|publisher=University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa|date=20 July 2016|access-date=18 September 2016}}</ref>) was a professor of physics at the [[University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa]], a former director of the Free Electron Laser Laboratory at [[Duke University]], and formerly a professor (research) at Stanford University. He is best known for his development of the [[free-electron laser]] (FEL) at [[Stanford University]] in the 1970s.<ref>New Light: What is free electron laser, Isamu Sato, International Symposium of Maxillofacial and Oral regenerative biology in Okayama (2003)</ref><ref name="xxx">{{Cite journal | last1 = Madey | first1 = J. M. J. | title = Stimulated Emission of Bremsstrahlung in a Periodic Magnetic Field | doi = 10.1063/1.1660466 | journal = Journal of Applied Physics | volume = 42 | issue = 5 | pages = 1906–1913 | year = 1971 | bibcode = 1971JAP....42.1906M }}</ref>

Raised in [[Clark, New Jersey]], Madey and his older brother Jules took an early interest in ham radio. In 1956, when John was 13 and Jules was 16, they began relaying communications from the south pole to families and friends in the United States.<ref>
{{cite news |title=United States Antarctic Program |author=Elaine Hood |publisher=United States Government
|url=http://antarcticsun.usap.gov/features/contentHandler.cfm?id=1688 |access-date=2013-10-28}}</ref>  While an undergraduate at the [[California Institute of Technology]], he had a discussion where the question came up as to whether or not it was possible to enhance the transition rate for [[bremsstrahlung]] through [[stimulated emission]].<ref>
{{cite web |title=Advancing the Laser |publisher=[[SPIE]]
|url=http://spie.org/Documents/AboutSPIE/SPIE%20Laser%20Luminaries.pdf |access-date=2013-10-28}}</ref>  Madey received a BS degree in physics and a MS degree in Quantum Electronics from the California Institute of Technology in 1964 and 1965. He continued thinking about the stimulated emission question while working on his doctoral degree at Stanford, when he invented the free-electron laser. He was awarded a PhD in 1970, and appointed  as Professor (Research) of Electrical Engineering in 1986.<ref>{{cite news
|title=Physicist John Madey to be awarded the Robert R. Wilson Prize in 2012 |date=November 2, 2011
|publisher=University of Hawaii at Mānoa
|url=http://www.hawaii.edu/news/article.php?aId=4765 |access-date=2013-10-28}}</ref>

[[File:Free electron laser patent.tif|thumb|Madey's free-electron laser patent (US 5130994), filed June 25, 1991, issued July 14, 1992]]
Stanford University refused to [[patent]] this idea so Madey filed for a patent on his own.{{citation needed|date=October 2013}} In the following years, he developed an innovative laser research program which was highly regarded in the [[scientific community]]. An opportunity arose for Madey to leave Stanford, taking a [[tenure]]d position at the Physics Department of Duke University, which Madey accepted in 1988, moving his FEL research laboratory with him in 1989. This laboratory contained substantial equipment which required Duke to build an addition to its physics building to house the lab. In addition, while at Stanford, Madey had obtained sole ownership of two patents practiced by some of the equipment in the FEL lab.

==Patent litigation==
At Duke, Madey served for almost a decade as director of the FEL lab.  During that time the lab continued to achieve success both in securing [[research funding]] and in generating scientific breakthroughs.  A dispute arose, however, between Madey and Duke. Duke contends that, despite his scientific prowess, Madey had ineffectively managed the lab, resulting in a negative external review of the science and management in his lab.<ref>{{cite news
|author=Richard Rubin
|publisher=Duke University
|date=May 20, 1999
|newspaper=The Chronicle
|url=http://www.dukechronicle.com/articles/1999/05/20/university-hires-new-director-free-electron-laser-lab
|access-date=2013-10-24
|title=University hires new director for free electron laser lab
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131029203040/http://www.dukechronicle.com/articles/1999/05/20/university-hires-new-director-free-electron-laser-lab
|archive-date=October 29, 2013
|url-status=dead}}</ref> Madey contends that Duke sought to use the lab's equipment for research areas outside the allocated scope of certain government funding, and that when he objected, Duke sought to remove him as lab director.  Duke eventually removed Madey as director of the lab in 1997.  The removal is not at issue in this appeal, however, it is the genesis of a unique [[patent infringement]] case.  As a result of his removal from the directorship, Madey resigned from Duke in 1998.  Duke, however, continued to operate some of the equipment in the lab. Madey then sued Duke for patent infringement of his two patents, and brought a variety of other claims.<ref>{{cite court
 |litigants = Madey v. Duke University
 |vol = 307
 |reporter = F.3d
 |opinion = 1351
 |pinpoint =
 |court = Court of Appeals, Federal Circuit
 |date = 2002
 |url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13577625967649928741&hl=en&as_sdt=2006
 |quote = Duke has conceded that at least some of its uses of Plaintiff's patents "unmistakably further its legitimate business objectives, including educating and enlightening students and faculty participating in these projects."}}</ref>

Initially, Madey suffered judicial setback, but later appeals courts found in his favor and made a historic judgment in his favor. In Madey v. Duke University, 307 F.3d 1351, 1362 (Fed. Cir. 2002)], the [[Federal Circuit Court of Appeals]] on October 3, 2002, effectively ended a 170-year-old practice of allowing scientists to freely borrow patented technologies for limited use in [[Research|basic research]] that is not aimed at commercial use.<ref>{{Cite journal |doi = 10.1126/science.299.5603.26a|title = INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY: Universities Ask Supreme Court to Reverse Patent Ruling|journal = Science|volume = 299|issue = 5603|pages = 26a–27|year = 2003|last1 = Malakoff|first1 = D.}}</ref><ref>
{{cite journal |author=Jennifer Miller
|journal=Duke Law and Technology Review
|publisher=Duke School of Law, Duke University |date=2003
|volume=2 |issue=1
|title=Sealing the Coffin on the Experimental Use Exception
|url=http://scholarship.law.duke.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1081&context=dltr
|access-date=2013-10-24}}</ref>

==Awards==
Madey was awarded the [[Stuart Ballantine Medal]] from [[The Franklin Institute]] in 1989.

Madey received the 2012 ''Robert R. Wilson Prize for Achievement in the Physics of Particle Accelerators'', from the [[American Physical Society]] ''"For the invention and first experimental demonstration of the free electron laser and important contributions to its conceptual development."''<ref>{{cite web
|title=2012 Robert R. Wilson Prize for Achievement in the Physics of Particle Accelerators Recipient
|publisher=American Physical Society |access-date=2013-10-28
|url=http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Madey&first_nm=John&year=2012}}</ref>

Madey was awarded the Willis E. Lamb Award for Laser Science and Quantum Optics in 2016.<ref>
{{Citation | url = http://www.lambaward.org/|title=Willis E. Lamb Award}}</ref>
